item.title: A Former Appliance Store Becomes a Hong Kong Cocktail Bar
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting, transformational design, and cultural context.

Good design is all about transformation and turning the everyday into memorable spaces. Kevin Yiu, principal at Minus Workshop, did just that with his recent conversion of a former appliance store into Mius, a cocktail bar in Hong Kong.

Nestled at 29 Gough Street in the SoHo district, the space reflects owner Shelley Tai’s belief in simple things done right, from libations that honor the classics to comfort food without complication. “Her desire for a genuine neighborhood bar challenged me to translate that specific vibe into spatial design,” Yiu explains.

Yiu embraced mid-century modern design, and with only eight months to complete the project, he turned constraints into assets. High ceilings and a curated system of leather blinds capture sunlight by day, then offer layered illumination in the evening. A low structural beam clad in oak now doubles as an element that guides circulation and visually organizes the spaces. Electrical and mechanical systems remain hidden by joinery, which still allows access for maintenance.

The material palette blends a range of contrasting textures. Wood veneer adds an organic appeal, while bronze and silver metals cast a subtle sheen, paired with shades of copper and brown. Minimal paint, rather than the artificial brightness of lacquer, keeps the aesthetic grounded.

The 14-foot stainless steel bar top is both a statement piece and a functional surface that integrates essential equipment for the staff. Slabs of travertine form high tables where guests enjoy small plates or signature drinks. Reflective accents and strategic voids make the compact interior look more expansive.

Yiu decided to split bar operations across four counters to ease peak-hour congestion, keeping service clean and efficient. The queue flows from the front to the bar, with stools framing the activity in the main area.

A floating chandelier by Lee Broom features celestial orbs that cast even light over the crowd. Plush velvet curtains drape over storage room doorways, and accent lamps round out a style that is bespoke but never stuffy.

For Yiu, it is a place that unfolds quietly, meant to be savored like the fare on the menu. “Mius is a sanctuary of simplicity, designed with a contemplative approach, which allows the interior architecture to elevate the hospitality experience,” he says.

item.title: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical innovation in design workflow, useful vocabulary.

Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow

Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.

Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.

As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.

From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.

Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule “clean” as the design is fleshed out.

Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.

The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.

Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.

The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.

Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.

In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.

The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.

If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.

Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.

For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.

The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.

This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.

Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.

Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.

The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.

The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.

The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.

To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

item.title: This week the highly anticipated London Museum opened
item.description:

Why it is here: Comprehensive overview of museum openings, diverse content.

This week the highly anticipated London Museum opened

This week on Dezeen, we revealed the transformation of London’s 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum, completed by architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects.

Ten years in the making, the renovated Victorian market building now contains two main gallery spaces – one an airy open space and the other a subterranean exhibition at Roman street level – displaying artefacts from London’s history.

Another major museum that opened this week is Kanal in Brussels, which at 40,000 square metres, claims to be “Europe’s largest museum development”.

Atelier Kanal renovated the 1930s Citroën Garage and added three volumes within its structure to form the modern art and architecture museum, which features exhibitions developed with Paris’s Centre Pompidou.

In design news, Swedish retailer IKEA announced a deep, reddish-purple hue as its Colour of the Year for 2027.

Named Wild Fig, IKEA said the colour “unexpectedly fits in”, whether used in furnishings, accessories, or painted across entire walls.

Following the announcement of this year’s Dezeen Awards winners, we rounded up key projects completed by the awards’ emerging designers of the year.

Notable projects by emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa include a house in Japan and a bathing pavilion designed for the Osaka World Expo 2025.

Projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner include sculptural lighting made from secondhand glassware and afro combs.

Also this week, the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) announced the Edinburgh Futures Institute as the winner of the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland for 2026.

UK studio Bennetts Associates renovated the Category A-listed Victorian building, formerly an infirmary, and integrated new teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.

Popular projects this week include an art gallery in Doha adorned with kaleidoscopic patterns, a house in Maryland punctured with lightwells, and a renovated home in Yorkshire designed to feel like a wine bar.

Following our investigation into greenwashing claims of putting trees on buildings, our podcast this week looked at why wooded buildings are so controversial.
